At the population level, no conditioning implies the inequality for the distribution of all eligible fresh entrants under every attrition process, so a violation is evidence against the maintained model---refreshment validity, comparable coding, for an ordered item whose categories the stayers all report deterministic monotone measurement, and, for the complete-case ratio, the two item-response requirements above---that no attrition process removes (@cor-discrete). We report these ratios as descriptive complete-case diagnostics. Fresh-sample item nonresponse can generate a flag even without conditioning; interpreting the ratios through @cor-discrete additionally requires representative item completion within comparable eligible subgroups, and sampling calibration alone does not establish that requirement. Nor does an infinite or large *sample* ratio show that a population mass is zero or that the population inequality fails: the criterion is a maximum of estimated ratios whose sampling error is not calibrated here, rare categories inflate it (the denominator is the fresh cohort's share of the category, estimated from at most 963 entrants and from far fewer for subgroup items, whose $\hat p$ also carries the error of the estimated subgroup share), and no multiplicity adjustment is applied across items. A one-sided confidence bound on the maximal ratio, with multiplicity control across items, is the appropriate inferential version and is left to future work.

# Discussion

The results delimit a division of labour. What a refreshment sample cannot do by itself is separate conditioning from attrition selection when the location set is nondegenerate: @thm-sharp gives the exact residual ambiguity, which, on the latent-outcome support, vanishes without attrition and, under outcome-independent attrition, whenever the refreshment density has tails thinner than exponential (@cor-independent). Within a cohort and without restrictions linking waves, the panel's own history does not narrow it (@thm-multiwave), so, within the maintained model, additional identifying restrictions must exclude otherwise feasible completions. What a refreshment sample can do is threefold: bound the ambiguity by an observable density-ratio criterion---the Horowitz--Manski interval for an unrestricted map (@cor-meanbounds), the location set of @thm-bounds, the mass inequality for an item whose categories are all reported (@cor-discrete); shrink it with covariates (@prp-covariates) and with negative controls under a transport restriction; and, with a negative-control battery at each refreshment and the transport restriction (A2) with a known loading, remove it at the tenures observed at refreshment episodes. The no-conditioning restriction that the refreshment-sample attrition literature maintains [@hirano2001; @deng2013] selects one point of a set whose extent the data reveal, and whose plug-in width, @rem-trim warns, depends on where the analyst stops trusting the tails.

Three points bear on practice. First, @dasetal2011 [main text and online Appendix 1] show that the same entry-wave functional identifies population or survivor conditioning effects under different stationarity assumptions. The general-mean formulation here (B4 for the survivor effect) preserves that distinction, which is important when conditioning effects are heterogeneous: the two readings coincide under homogeneous effects and differ by the composition term $\mathbb{E}[\tau_i \mid S] - \mathbb{E}[\tau_i]$ otherwise (Simulation 3), so reports of entry-wave-corrected estimates should state which target they intend. Second, the diagnostics are compatibility checks among the maintained restrictions B1--B5, not classifiers. When non-stationary and state-dependent attrition are both present, the estimator with the smallest bias in Simulation 3 is survival matching, whose restriction both failures violate, because the two failures bias it in opposite directions; and under stationary state dependence in model (M), $\mathcal{T}_{\mathrm{NS}}$ has no power at all. A rejection is evidence that the set of restrictions is inconsistent, to be followed by the overidentification tests of @thm-tworef(c). Third, the identified set of the conditioning path on a staggered trapezoid has dimension at least the stride of the refreshment schedule, and more when the follow-up of the last cohort is short; on irregular supports it can be larger or smaller, and the rank computation of @thm-rank, not a closed-form condition, is the general check.

The deterministic monotone-map model serves continuous items. For items whose categories are all reported it is a specification test (@cor-discrete), and response-style shifts of the kind reported in @sec-implementation, if they reflect conditioning, are a stochastic partial merging of categories that the deterministic model does not represent. Neither the application of the binary analysis of @dasetal2011 to each event $\{Y > a\}$, which they suggest for non-binary outcomes [p. 36], nor a joint distributional treatment of stochastic conditioning on ordered categories is attempted here.

Our recommendations for panels with refreshment designs are therefore: report the identified set rather than assuming it away, stating the trim and slack of any plug-in version; report survivor and population targets separately when effects may be heterogeneous; design panels with at least two refreshments, an entry-wave negative-control battery, and where possible a *repeated tenure* across refreshment episodes, which in the location family adds a direct test of stationary selection; compute the rank of a proposed schedule before fielding it; choose refreshment waves whose spacings have no common divisor and follow the last refreshment cohort long enough (for the panel of @sec-implementation, an entry at an even wave followed for at least three waves); and release disclosure-approved rotation-group summaries alongside balanced aggregates. These are identification decisions that are usually taken on other grounds.

# Appendix: Simulation Evidence (ADEMP) {#sec-ademp}

Three simulation studies, reported in the ADEMP format, examine the finite-sample content of the results, and three deterministic scripts verify the worked examples, the counterexamples, and the design-rank statements. Code and outputs are in the `sims/` folder of the replication archive: the scripts `sim1_bounds.R`, `sim2_multicohort.R` and `sim3_designs.R`, and the checks `check_funnel_examples.R`, `check_multiwave_completion.R` and `check_design_rank.py`. No confidential data are involved. `check_manuscript_values.R`, also in `sims/`, asserts every simulation value quoted in the text and tables against a named cell of the output files, with the estimand and units of each. The data-generating processes and estimands below are those implemented in the archived scripts.

**Simulation 1 (@thm-sharp, @cor-funnel, @thm-bounds: a relaxed plug-in procedure).** *Data-generating mechanism*: bivariate Gaussian $(Y_1, Y_2^{*})$ with unit variances and $\rho = .5$; logistic outcome selection $\pi = \Lambda(a + \beta Y_2^{*})$ with $\beta \in \{0, .3, .6\}$ and $a$ tuned to retention $p \in \{.6, .8\}$; location conditioning $h \in \{0, .2\}$; $n = 4{,}000$ plus a refreshment sample of $2{,}000$; 200 replications per cell (in two cells one replication produced an empty plug-in set and is excluded from the set summaries). *Estimand*: $h$. *Methods*: a relaxed plug-in set $\{h' : \sup_{y} \hat p\, \hat q(y + h')/\hat f_2(y) \le 1 + \kappa\}$ with kernel densities, the supremum taken over the support trimmed at $10\%$ of the refreshment density's mode, slack $\kappa = .10$, and candidates $h' \in [-1, 1.5]$ on a grid of step $.01$ that contains the true values; the naive comparator is quantile alignment ignoring attrition. As population benchmarks the script computes, without sampling, the identified set of @thm-bounds for the same process, $h + [0, \Delta^{*}]$ (a point when $\beta = 0$), and the population analogue of the relaxed procedure (the same trim and slack applied to the true densities). *Performance*: The naive estimator's bias is essentially zero at $\beta = 0$ (at most $.004$ in absolute value), $.056$--$.058$ at $\beta = .3$ and $.114$--$.116$ at $\beta = .6$ when $p = .8$, and $.116$--$.118$ and $.218$--$.220$ when $p = .6$: raising retention from $.6$ to $.8$ halves it. The population identified sets have widths $0$, $.145$ and $.262$ at $p = .8$ and $0$, $.260$ and $.489$ at $p = .6$ for $\beta = 0, .3, .6$. The relaxed plug-in sets are wider---mean widths $.25$--$.32$ at $p = .8$ and $.58$--$.68$ at $p = .6$---and positive at $\beta = 0$, where the identified set is a point. Their widths track those of the population analogue of the relaxed procedure ($.31$--$.38$ at $p = .8$, $.61$--$.71$ at $p = .6$), so they are properties of the trim and the slack, not of the identified set (@rem-trim), and @fig-funnel reports them as such. Coverage of the true $h$ by the relaxed plug-in set, counting an endpoint equal to the truth as covering it, is $.930$--$1$ at $p = .6$ and $.760$--$.965$ at $p = .8$, falling with $\beta$; a uniformly valid version requires inference-aware calibration of the slack, in the spirit of intersection-bounds methods, which we leave to future work.

![Relaxed plug-in sets and population identified sets, Simulation 1, true $h = 0.2$. Bars: mean over 200 replications of the relaxed plug-in set (support trimmed at 10% of the refreshment density's mode, slack 0.10). Dark segments: the population identified set of @thm-bounds for the same data-generating process (open squares: a single point). Dots: mean naive quantile-alignment estimate. The plug-in widths reflect the trim and the slack; the population sets widen with selection strength and narrow with retention.](figures/fig1_funnel.png){#fig-funnel}

**Simulation 2 (@thm-tworef, @cor-generational).** *Data-generating mechanism*: three cohorts entering at waves 1, 5 and 13 ($n = 3{,}000$ each), compared at wave 13; a latent trait $u_i \sim N(0,1)$ and per-wave retention $\Lambda(1.6 + 0.6u_i)$, so that the first cohort has passed twelve response decisions and the second eight; target item $y = g_e + \tau(s) + u + e$ with $e \sim N(0,1)$ and $\tau(s) = .15(1 - e^{-(s-1)/4})$; a $K = 23$ negative-control battery measured at entry, $x_k = .6u + \eta_k$; a generational variant adds a cohort effect $g = .35$ to the wave-13 entrants' target item; a contaminated variant adds recall drift $.15$ to three battery items of the first cohort; 300 replications. *Estimands*, in units of the target's population standard deviation $\sqrt 2$: the incumbent increment $(\tau(13) - \tau(9))/\sqrt2 = .15(e^{-2} - e^{-3})/\sqrt2 = .0091$ and the level contrast $(\tau(13) - \tau(1))/\sqrt2 = .1008$. *Methods*: contrasts of survivors' raw means, divided by $\sqrt 2$; negative-control corrections subtract $\Gamma$ times the mean raw battery contrast of the same pair of cohorts, with the true raw loading $\Gamma = 1/.6$ (exact (A2)) or a unit loading on the population-standardized scale ($\Gamma = \sqrt2/\sqrt{1.36}$, an under-correction by the factor $.73$); a screened correction removes items flagged by a per-item outlier screen ($|z| > 2.5$, centred at the median item contrast) before pooling by the mean, and a median-pooled correction uses the median item contrast. The script also computes the population limit of each estimator by numerical integration. *Performance*: the naive increment is biased by $.152$ (population limit $.151$) from differential selection; the correction with the true loading has bias $.002$ (Monte Carlo standard error $.002$; population limit zero) and RMSE $.042$; the unit loading leaves $.043$ (limit $.041$)---a reminder that (A2) is a substantive assumption whose miscalibration under-corrects proportionally. The corrected level contrast has bias $.003$ (standard error $.002$) in the age-matched design and $-.250$ in the generational design, where the corrected contrast contains $-g/\sqrt2 = -.247$; the incumbent increment stays unbiased there ($-.000$). The battery-homogeneity $Q$ test rejects at $.003$--$.007$ at nominal $.05$ without drift and at $.34$ with three drifted items; the screen flags at least one of the three drifted items in $68\%$ of replications, against $2\%$ for the same three items without drift, and flags an undrifted item at a per-item rate below $.01$. Undetected drift contaminates the mean-pooled correction (bias $-.017$); screening before pooling ($-.007$) and median pooling ($-.006$) reduce it.

**Simulation 3 (constructive designs and diagnostics; @sec-constructive--@sec-diagnostics).** *Data-generating mechanism*: model (M) of @prp-fail with a continuing cohort of $n_{\text{old}} = 4{,}800$ entering at wave 1 and a fresh cohort of $n_{\text{new}} = 960$ entering at wave 5 (dose $k = 4$); latent outcome $Y^{*}_{it} = 0.5X_i + 0.5U_i + \varepsilon_{it}$ with $X_i \sim$ Bernoulli$(.5)$, $U_i \sim N(0,1)$, $\varepsilon_{it} \sim N(0,1)$ independent across waves, untreated standard deviation $1.146$; a heterogeneous conditioning shift $\tau_i(s) = 0.30\{1 - e^{-(s-1)/4}\}(1 + \gamma U_i)$ whose population mean at $s = 5$ is $0.190$ ($0.166$ standard deviations); and a dropout logit $-2.2 + a_X X_i + b_w U_i + a_E\varepsilon_{iw}$ for the decision taken at wave $w$. Six regimes: MCAR; MAR on $X$ ($a_X = .8$); MNAR on the trait ($a_X = .4$, $b_w = .8$); non-stationary MNAR on the trait, in which the trait coefficient is $1.4$ at the continuing cohort's waves before the comparison wave and $.8$ at every other wave of both cohorts, so that trait selection is *stronger* in the continuing cohort's selection period; state-dependent MNAR ($a_X = .4$, $b_w = .4$, $a_E = .8$); and both failures together. Heterogeneity is $\gamma = .3$ (survivor targets $h^{S}$ and $h^{S+}$ differ from the population shift and from each other, the case B5 excludes) or $\gamma = 0$. *Estimands*: $h^{S}$ (SM, EC, naive), $h^{S+}$ (SSM), the population shift (IPW). *Methods*: the five estimators with influence-function standard errors that include the estimated group shares (@sec-variance); the diagnostics $\mathcal{T}_{\mathrm{NS}}$ and $\mathcal{T}_{\mathrm{SD}}$ at the 5% level. *Performance measures*: bias against each estimator's own estimand and against the population shift, coverage of 95% intervals, rejection rates. $R = 1{,}000$ replications per regime and setting. The two settings of $\gamma$ within a regime use the same seed, so their data are identical apart from the shift (common random numbers) and paired differences isolate the effect of heterogeneity. Part D adds the variance experiments described below. Code: `sims/sim3_designs.R`.

| MNAR non-stationary | −.279 (.00) | **−.081 (.65)** | **−.068 (.76)** | −.002 (.95) | −.292 | **.623** | .078 |
| MNAR state-dependent | −.127 (.17) | **+.104 (.53)** | +.002 (.95) | **+.103 (.36)** | −.115 | .040 | **.993** |
| MNAR, both failures | −.292 (.00) | +.012 (.93) | **−.062 (.80)** | **+.078 (.59)** | −.306 | **.430** | **.945** |

: Simulation 3, bias against each estimator's own estimand in outcome units (95% coverage in parentheses) and rejection rates of the two diagnostics at the 5% level; 1,000 replications per regime. Monte Carlo standard errors of the biases are at most 0.002 and of the rejection rates at most 0.016. {#tbl-sim3}

The first five rows of @tbl-sim3 match @prp-fail(i)--(ii) row by row: survival matching fails under non-stationarity and under state dependence, symmetric matching only under non-stationarity, the entry-wave correction only under state dependence, and under state dependence survival matching and the entry-wave correction carry the same bias ($+.104$ and $+.103$), so that $\mathcal{T}_{\mathrm{NS}}$ keeps its nominal size there. The sixth row is a case the diagnostics cannot classify: with both failures present, $\mathcal{T}_{\mathrm{SD}}$ rejects almost always and $\mathcal{T}_{\mathrm{NS}}$ less than half the time, and the estimator with the smallest bias is survival matching---not because its restriction holds but because the two failures bias it in opposite directions. A rejection is evidence of incompatibility among the maintained restrictions, and a non-rejection of one statistic is not evidence that the corresponding restriction holds.

*Survivor versus population targets (@prp-ec).* This part illustrates, for a continuous outcome, the distinction that @dasetal2011 [p. 41, and online Appendix 1, pp. 27--28] draw for binary items between the population and the survivor target of the same functional. With heterogeneous shifts ($\gamma = 0.3$), dropout increases with $U$, so the survivors carry *smaller* shifts than the population: under MNAR on the trait the survivor target averages $.170$ against a population shift of $.190$. The entry-wave correction is unbiased for the survivor effect $h^{S}$ ($-.001$) and biased for the population shift ($-.021$, or 11% of $\tau(5)$); with homogeneous shifts ($\gamma = 0$) the two targets coincide and the population bias is $-.001$. Because the two settings share their data, the paired difference of the population biases, $-.020$, is the composition term $\mathbb{E}[\tau_i \mid S] - \mathbb{E}[\tau_i]$ up to a Monte Carlo error below $.0001$. Read as an estimate of the population effect---the target of their Assumption 3, a stationarity-of-attrition-bias assumption on the *conditioned* outcome, which fails in this design because survival selects on the heterogeneity of the shift---the functional is off by that composition term; read as an estimate of $h^{S}$ under B4 (their Assumption 3$^{\mathrm{Alt}}$ for a binary item), it is unbiased here. Survival matching and symmetric matching show the same gap of about $.02$ between their survivor and population readings. The paired comparison also shows the role of B5: the $\mathcal{T}_{\mathrm{SD}}$ rejection rate under MNAR on the trait is $.056$ with heterogeneous shifts and $.044$ when the composition term $h^{S+} - h^{S}$ is switched off (paired difference $.012$, Monte Carlo standard error $.005$).

*Variance (@sec-variance).* In Part A the share terms are small relative to the within-group variances, and the coverage of the entry-wave correction is essentially the same with and without them (for example $.945$ and $.944$ under MNAR on the trait). Part D shows when they matter. In D1, a null experiment with well-separated groups (entry and comparison responses both equal to $U + N(0, .1^2)$ with $U \sim$ Bernoulli$(.5)$, survival $S = U$ in both cohorts, 500 entrants per cohort, no conditioning, 5,000 replications), the influence-function variance of the entry-wave correction averages $.00104$, against an empirical variance of $.00106$ and a theoretical value of $.00104$, and gives coverage $.947$ and a $\mathcal{T}_{\mathrm{NS}}$ rejection rate of $.056$; the within-group formula without share terms averages $.00054$ and gives $.839$ and $.706$. In D2, an exact counterexample ($E = S$, $Y = 1$ among survivors, a constant fresh outcome), the entry-wave estimate equals the survival share $\hat p$, whose variance is $p(1-p)/n$; the influence-function estimate is its plug-in version $\hat p(1 - \hat p)/n$, while the within-group formula returns zero. In D3, a person-level bootstrap within cohort that recomputes every arm and every share (200 replications, 200 resamples each) agrees with the influence-function standard errors to within one per cent in D1 and in the MNAR-trait and MNAR-state regimes.

**Deterministic checks (no sampling).** `check_funnel_examples.R` reproduces, on a fine grid with stated tolerances, the identified set $\{-1\}$ for $f_2 = N(0,1)$, $Q = N(-1,1)$, $p = .5$; the attainment of $\Delta^{*} = \beta\sigma^2$ in the Gaussian--logistic example at $\alpha = -1$; the point $\{0\}$ under outcome-independent attrition with Gaussian tails; the Laplace and logistic half-widths $\log(1/p)$ and the Cauchy half-widths $(1-p)/\sqrt p$; the central-binding example after @cor-funnel at $\sigma = .5$ and $.8$; the disconnected identified sets of the modulated Cauchy and logistic densities of @cor-independent, together with the exponential-tail outer bound and the failure of the closed form without the Lipschitz condition; the Lipschitz neighbourhood of @cor-independent(iii); the discrete examples of @cor-discrete; the general-map example of @cor-repeated; the retention-only covariate of @prp-covariates; and a case in which the per-pair outer bound of @thm-tworef(a) is strictly larger than the common-loading set (a Laplace episode with $C_1 = 0$, $N_1 = 1$ and a Gaussian episode with $C_2 = 10$, $N_2 = 1$, both at $p = .5$, with $\Gamma \in [0, 1]$: the Gaussian episode forces $\Gamma = 0$, so the common-loading set for the first episode is $\{0\}$ rather than $[-\log 2, 0]$; block 11 of the script); and the example following @thm-tworef, in which the loading set computed from the margins, $[0, .817]$, strictly contains the set under the joint version of (A1), $[0, .263]$ (block 12). `check_multiwave_completion.R` enumerates, without sampling, a four-wave cohort on the latent lattice $\{-5, \dots, 5\}$ with a binary entry-only negative control, all eight response patterns (interrupted ones included), true conditioning by integer location shifts $(0, 1, 0, 1)$, and a selection kernel that depends on the whole latent path including the never-reported coordinates and that excludes the lowest latent value from responding at wave 4. For every candidate map $c'_4 = c_4 + \epsilon$, $\epsilon \in \{-3, \dots, 3\}$, with one arbitrary choice of candidate maps at the intermediate waves (shifts of $+1$ and $-1$ at waves 2 and 3), the completion of @lem-seqcompletion is constructed explicitly. Exactly one non-trivial candidate, $\epsilon = +1$, satisfies the wave-4 domination inequality; for it and for $\epsilon = 0$ every pattern sub-measure, the entry marginal including the negative control, and the refreshment marginal are reproduced within the script's tolerance of $10^{-10}$, the kernel is a valid Markov kernel, the survivors' latent mean at wave 4 moves by $-\epsilon$, and the negative-control contrast does not move; for every other $\epsilon$ the leftover $L_4$ has a negative entry. Restricting the same example to monotone patterns verifies the sequential form $\pi'_j = dN_{j+1}/dN_j$. The script also enumerates all 35 weakly increasing maps on four categories and confirms in every instance that the mass criterion @eq-mass coincides with a linear-programming feasibility test, with the identity as the sole feasible map when all categories are reported and non-identity maps feasible only when a category goes unreported; and it confirms the Gaussian widths of @cor-meanbounds ($.390$, $.700$, $1.288$, $1.596$ at $p = .9, .8, .6, .5$) by closed form, numerical integration, and a linear programme on a grid. `check_design_rank.py` computes, in exact rational arithmetic, the rank and the projected kernel of every design quoted in @sec-design and @tbl-strides, the example of @thm-rank(iii) and its null vector, the four-cohort example of @prp-stride(iii), the effect of level and plateau anchors on the Japanese panel's support, and, on all 2,214 staggered trapezoids with three to five cohorts, first entry at wave 1, later entries in $\{2, \dots, 10\}$ and up to eight periods of follow-up, the component count, the sufficient follow-up condition, the exact three-cohort formula and the upper bound of the companion identification paper's Lemma 1. On 65 of these designs every pair of observed tenures is linked through tenures observed in common periods although the identified set is larger than $d$.

# Appendix: Variance of the Design Estimators {#sec-variance}

Each estimator of @sec-constructive and each diagnostic of @sec-diagnostics is a difference of subset means computed within two independent cohorts. For a cohort of $n$ persons and a subset indicator $B_i$, the mean $\bar Y_B = \sum_i B_i Y_i / \sum_i B_i$ has influence function $\psi_i = B_i(Y_i - \mu_B)/\Pr(B)$; a linear combination of subset means within the cohort has the corresponding combination of influence functions, and its variance is estimated by $\sum_i \hat\psi_i^2/n^2$. For the entry-wave correction, with $S$ survival through $t$, $E$ the entry response and $Y$ the response at $t$, the continuing-cohort component $\hat A = \bar Y_S - (\bar E_S - \bar E)$ satisfies
$$
n\,\mathrm{Var}(\hat A) \;\approx\; \frac{\mathrm{Var}\{Y - (1-p)E \mid S\}}{p} \;+\; (1-p)\,\mathrm{Var}(E \mid \text{NS}) \;+\; p(1-p)\,(\mu_{E,S} - \mu_{E,\text{NS}})^2 ,
$$
where the last term comes from estimating the survivors' share $p$; a variance computed conditionally on the group sizes omits it. The diagnostics $\mathcal{T}_{\mathrm{NS}} = (\bar E_S - \bar E) - (\bar Y_{m} - \bar Y)$ and $\mathcal{T}_{\mathrm{SD}} = (\bar Y_{S+} - \bar Y_S) - (\bar Y_{m+1} - \bar Y_{m})$, where $\bar Y_{S+}$ averages the continuing survivors who also respond at $t+1$ and $\bar Y_m$, $\bar Y_{m+1}$ the fresh respondents who go on to respond for $k$ and $k+1$ further waves, contain the analogous share terms in both cohorts. A person-level bootstrap within cohort that recomputes every arm and every share targets the same variance. Simulation 3 and version 0.1.4 of the R package `panelcond` use the influence-function formulas; the empirical results of @sec-implementation use the bootstrap.

# Data and code availability {.unnumbered}

The simulations and deterministic checks generate their own data; no restricted data are needed to reproduce the appendix. Their code and outputs, the figure script, and the manuscript source are in the replication archive at <https://github.com/sokubo/paper-refreshment-designs-replication>; the version corresponding to this manuscript is tag `paper-v0.7` (computational commit `7480833`). The archive's README maps each table, figure and quoted simulation value to the script and output file that produce it, and `sims/check_manuscript_values.R` asserts those values against named output cells. The empirical illustration of @sec-implementation uses the integrated release (waves 1--19) of the Japanese Life Course Panel Surveys (JLPS) distributed to participants of the survey project; the microdata cannot be redistributed. Other researchers can apply for JLPS releases to the SSJDA Data Archive of the Center for Social Research and Data Archives, Institute of Social Science, The University of Tokyo (at the time of writing, the current releases are the study numbers PY160 and PM160); those releases differ from the integrated file, so an analysis of them with the archived code is a re-analysis with the same design and definitions rather than a replication. The archive contains the code that reads the licensed files and produces every aggregate quoted in @sec-implementation (`kit/R/`), a document stating the access route, the variables and the recoding (`kit/KIT_README.md`), and a synthetic data set with the outputs the code produces on it, so that the workflow for the 2011 episode can be run end to end without the licensed data; the scripts for the 2019 negative-control battery need the confidential map from items to variables and are not exercised by the synthetic example. Every script reads one explicitly named input file and records its name and SHA-256; `kit/KIT_README.md` gives the file name and fingerprint of the input behind @sec-implementation, and `kit/check_manuscript_values_T2.R` reproduces every quoted aggregate from the aggregate outputs after checking that all of them record that input. The aggregate outputs computed from the licensed data are reported in the paper (@sec-implementation, @tbl-ncbattery) and are not otherwise redistributed. The R package `panelcond`, version 0.1.4 (<https://github.com/sokubo/panelcond>, tag `v0.1.4`), implements the estimators, the diagnostics, the variance formulas of @sec-variance and the design-rank calculation; the design run behind @sec-implementation used its version 0.1.2, which differs from 0.1.4 only in analytic standard errors that no quoted number uses (all come from the person bootstrap).
